title: Two killed in Houthi attack on airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, authorities say
description: Yemen's Houthi movement has said it carried out an attack on an airport in eastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, which Saudi authorities said kil
body: Yemen's Houthi movement has said it carried out an attack on an airport in eastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, which Saudi authorities said killed two people and injured eight others.The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation identified those killed at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam as a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident.It did not say what type of attack occurred, but the Iran-backed Houthis said on Thursday that the airport was one of the sites they had targeted with drones and missiles over the previous 48 hours.Two more people were killed on Wednesday morning by debris from a drone that was intercepted elsewhere in Eastern Province, the Saudi energy ministry said.The drone was intercepted as it attempted to target a processing facility owned by Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco in the Shaybah oil field, where a contractor's vehicle was set ablaze, according to the ministry.It identified the dead as residents from the Philippines and Nepal.The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, did not claim the attack on the oil field.In addition to Dammam's airport, he said they had targeted the Saudi defence ministry's headquarters building in the capital, Riyadh, an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, and Abha International Airport in the south of the country.The Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis said four drones were intercepted over Eastern Province on Wednesday night, and that another four were intercepted over the provinces of Riyadh and Medina on Thursday.At least 21 people have now been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.The Houthis also reiterated on Thursday that they had attacked Saudi Arabia in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen.Houthi-run media reported on Wednesday night that at least six people had been killed and 11 injured in air and artillery strikes over the previous 24 hours.According to the Houthi-run health ministry, 155 civilians have been killed since Yemen's devastating civil war flared up three months ago.The government's health ministry has said at least 1,574 people have been killed in the conflict over the same period.The fighting has also displaced more than 256,000 people.The war began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated the next year, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities, and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.Earlier this month, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a counter-offensive with Saudi air support.However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib, al-Jawf, Dhale and Shabwa provinces.

schema.headline: Two killed in Houthi attack on airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, authorities say

title: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
description: Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires.Th
body: Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires.The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November.The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes.He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure.California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in California was less than 1%, external each year.Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe. Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board. It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed.In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal.Through what's known as a stock split announced by the company on Wednesday, Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings.Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value.The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California.Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence."The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii.After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring.Layoffs have continued into this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers.   Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools.  With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company.  Major tech companies are set to spend an estimated $1 trillion, external this year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, like data centres.Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year.  It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in.And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work.The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday.Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company.

schema.headline: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax

title: Durban attack: Crowd of 50 beats foreigner to death in South Africa
description: A foreign national has been beaten to death by a crowd of about 50 people in Durban, South Africa, police say.According to police, the unidentified ma
body: A foreign national has been beaten to death by a crowd of about 50 people in Durban, South Africa, police say.According to police, the unidentified man, believed to be in his late 30s or early 40s, was first approached by two men by the roadside before being assaulted by a larger group. He was pronounced dead at the scene.Police have launched an investigation into the murder, with the motive yet to be established.The killing follows a wave of protests against immigrants in South Africa this year, some of which have turned violent. Earlier this month, shops and cars were set on fire in Durban, as well as Soweto, near Johannesburg.Provincial police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda told the BBC they cannot speculate on the motive for the killing in Durban and that more information would be shared once verified.The government has urged the demonstrators to act peacefully, while also accepting the need for immigration reforms. It says tens of thousands of foreign nationals have been deported or repatriated since it launched a crackdown earlier this year.One of the groups behind the protests, March and March, had initially set a deadline of 30 June for all undocumented migrants to leave South Africa.Several protests were held ahead of that deadline, with reports of attacks on people from other African countries.These prompted several countries, including Zimbabwe, Nigeria and Ghana, to take steps to repatriate their citizens amid fears of further violence.Nigeria accused South African authorities of responsibility for the deaths of two of its citizens that month.Ghana also confirmed the death of a citizen, Bashiru Isak, a father of three who was fatally shot in Cape Town during demonstrations targeting foreign nationals. His death led to a diplomatic row with South Africa, which said the scale of the violence had been exaggerated.One of the leaders of the March and March movement, Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, denied that she was xenophobic."We can't be living with these people for so many years and now when we say it is too much, it is enough, we are told that we are xenophobic," she told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme.South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals.The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce.Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence.Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities.Additional reporting by Pumza Fihlani in Johannesburg

schema.headline: Durban attack: Crowd of 50 beats foreigner to death in South Africa

title: Ilhan Omar says 'bizarre' pre-dawn raid on her home is forcing her to move out
description: Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar has said she can no longer live in her Washington DC home after it was searched by federal agents last week, feari
body: Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar has said she can no longer live in her Washington DC home after it was searched by federal agents last week, fearing her address has been exposed after the raid."With the death threats that I deal with, it's not, it's no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids," she told MS Now, external. In Omar's first public interview since the pre-dawn search of her home, she detailed how Homeland Security Investigations agents seized over a dozen items, including cell phones and notebooks, as part of an investigation. The government has not said what crime Omar is accused of but that the raid was "part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation".The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya.More than a dozen subpoenas have also been issued to members of Omar's family, as part of the investigation, and it was reported that her personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized.Recalling the hourslong raid of her home with MS Now, Omar said: "It obviously did freak all of us out." Omar said agents began "pounding on the doors" of her home at around 06:00 EDT (11:00 BST) on 12 October, startling her and her husband, who were both in bed."We were screaming," she said, as the couple ran downstairs to see what was happening, calling the incident "so bizarre".The Minnesota Democrat estimated that between15 to 25 agents encircled her home, all of whom she said "conducted themselves in a decent way".Agents presented Omar with a warrant at the door after she asked for one. She then watched from the couch as agents spent roughly five hours going from room to room, Omar said, leaving with a total of 17 items, including multiple cellphones, notebooks, and her husband's camera from the 1960s.The BBC contacted the Justice Department for comment after being referred by the DHS.Omar again criticised the government's investigation, suggesting that it was meant to be intimidating. Immediately following the raid last week, she posted a statement online where she called it "an outrageous abuse of power" and "weaponisation of federal law enforcement to target political enemies".Former President Barack Obama has also blasted the federal probe, saying in a lengthy statement that it was "so appalling".Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has long been a target of President Donald Trump's, who has repeatedly suggested she "go back" to Somalia.He has denied any involvement in her investigation, saying it has "nothing to do with me".At an Ohio rally in October, Trump referred to the search of her home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."The congresswoman, however, rejected the president's response, arguing that "he's got everything to do with it"."You know, this goes back to 2019 when he was screaming about the fact that, you know, I, I need to be sent back, I need to be deported."

schema.headline: Ilhan Omar says 'bizarre' pre-dawn raid on her home is forcing her to move out

title: How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?
description: Current polling puts incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in a tight race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, to become prime mini
body: Current polling puts incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in a tight race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, to become prime minister.Eisenkot's popularity stems partly from his military credentials and his relative newness in politics, having formed his Yashar Party only last year.He lost his son, a soldier, in the first months of the Gaza war, and served in Israel's war cabinet under Netanyahu until resigning in 2024 over disagreements about the conflict. He has built his campaign on calls for accountability over the security failures that led to 7 October.Other opposition leaders include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security and advocate permanent Israeli control over much of the occupied West Bank - and Yair Golan, a left-winger who supports Israel's withdrawal from large parts of the territory. Despite their differences, they could work with Eisenkot to form a government.Netanyahu's current government is the most right-wing in Israel's history. In order to remain in power, he will likely have to rely on the support of some of his existing far-right coalition partners. Some hold ultra-nationalist positions, such as calling for Israel to annex the West Bank and for the "migration" of Palestinians from Gaza - which could amount to the forced displacement of civilians. Some members of Netanyahu's own Likud party have also called for Palestinian "migration" from the territory. There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers. But all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them.A year on from the ceasefire in Gaza, Israel continues to carry out near-daily strikes on the territory - saying it is targeting Hamas operatives - and maintains control of more than half of it.More than 74,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza since 7 October 2023, according to the Hamas-run health ministry - whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.In the West Bank, attacks by Jewish settlers are at an all-time high, according to UN records, while Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law, are rapidly expanding.So for Palestinians, the shape of Israel's government is a major factor in their lives.On Gaza, the two leading camps - headed by Netanyahu and Eisenkot - hold similar positions - with both supporting Donald Trump's peace plan, which would see Hamas give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the territory. Eisenkot recently pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months, through military means if necessary.In the West Bank, Netanyahu's camp largely wants to continue with its policy of settlement expansion.Eisenkot supports Israeli settlements in general, but opposes proceeding with the controversial E1 settlement project which would, in effect, split the West Bank in two. He also wants to close some unauthorised settler outposts built on Palestinian land, create conditions for a final peace settlement with the Palestinians, and crack down on extremist Jewish settlers.For decades, many mainstream Israeli politicians advocated for a two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - although Netanyahu has long opposed it. But support for the idea has been declining for years. In this election, none of the leading Jewish parties are campaigning on it, and many have outright rejected it.

schema.headline: How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?

title: Rosenberg: Russia agrees to Ukraine talks but sees little to talk about in new peace push
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)BySteve RosenbergRussia
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)BySteve RosenbergRussia EditorReporting fromMoscowAfter two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard."In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace."I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said,  "but things are moving in that direction."All rather vague.It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Despite a "constructive" meeting between Witkoff and Zelensky in Oslo, Norway, the idea of a US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral summit does not seem to have taken holdIn recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky.That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader."Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says."Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?""Of course!"A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent.But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe."Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

schema.headline: Rosenberg: Russia agrees to Ukraine talks but sees little to talk about in new peace push

title: Paris extends curfew as Marseille and Lyon ban protests after riots
description: Paris is extending a partial curfew restricting movement in parts of the city until Monday, as Marseille and Lyon impose a total ban on protests this
body: Paris is extending a partial curfew restricting movement in parts of the city until Monday, as Marseille and Lyon impose a total ban on protests this weekend. The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums in the French capital will also be closed on Saturday as more demonstrations are expected.France is still reeling from major disorder at the weekend, when large protests against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed. In other parts of the country where protests have not been banned completely, only authorised union demonstrations will be allowed on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron said. Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest.France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise.Gérald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court.Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper. Police in Paris said its curfew in Place de la République, where protesters gathered last weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area will be extended until Monday.Movement will be prohibited in both areas from 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT) until 06:00 the following morning, the prefecture for the capital city said, adding that it had been ordered by Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.Public transport Marseille will be suspended on Saturday to try to prevent a repeat of the riots in the city.The city saw some of the worst violence last weekend and damage to more than 500 businesses. The prefecture for the Rhône region - which covers Marseille - said a curfew for minors would be extended to the entire population overnight on Saturday 24 October, from 23:00 until 05:00 (21:00 - 03:00 GMT). Similar announcements have been made in Nice in the south, Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east.Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday."The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced. "When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned."He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic". Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm.The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned.Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds.Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests. Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction.Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests. In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started. The iconic Place de la République was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc. The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year.

schema.headline: Paris extends curfew as Marseille and Lyon ban protests after riots

title: Trump says Musk has restored access to Ukraine's Starlink network
description: Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had still not been restored fully. Speaking at a press conferenc
body: Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had still not been restored fully. Speaking at a press conference, he said the speed "has not been restored to 400 [km/h; 250mph] yet", adding: "We are working on it."He continued: "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so."The Ukrainian president made the comments shortly before the Wall Street Journal, external reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink. The US outlet reported that Trump told Musk he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped at around 160km/h, according to officials. The speed limit made Ukraine's offensive drones and interceptors powerless against Russian attacks.The journal reported that the system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after their conversation. BBC News has not confirmed the Wall Street Journal's report. It has also contacted the White House and SpaceX to ask for an explanation.  Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing on 14 October. Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink which Ukraine uses for some of its operation. He said the system was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. The White House has repeatedly said it did not order access to be restricted.

schema.headline: Trump says Musk has restored access to Ukraine's Starlink network

title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to resume Ukraine peace talks
description: Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, bu
body: Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come."The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.  Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".He has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.He was also heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier.Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move.Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", and Zelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now".Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions to the US satellite internet network Starlink, which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia.US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an urgent investigation.

schema.headline: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to resume Ukraine peace talks

title: PHP: What is it and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble?
description: Figure caption, How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk?ByLiv McMahonTechnology reporter and Osmond ChiaBusiness reporterFor mo
body: Figure caption, How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk?ByLiv McMahonTechnology reporter and Osmond ChiaBusiness reporterFor more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet. It took AI to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI.OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".What is PHP?Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily.It stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, an open-source, back-end programming language which runs on a web server.Developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, PHP still powers lots of platforms today, including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites.When you visit a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.It has also been used to write a number of tools for building or speeding up the creation of web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.According to cyber-security firm Wiz, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites.It is maintained by a non-profit called the PHP Foundation, external, composed of individuals and companies which depend on the language and aim to ensure its "long-term prosperity".What is the vulnerability?A group of cyber-security researchers and organisations disclosed two vulnerabilities within PHP this week, which they warned could have the potential to upend sites across the internet.Cyber firms Wiz and Calif said the flaws – coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, with versions of PHP released over the last decade affected.Ryan Austin, a Calif researcher who helped uncover the security issues, told the BBC it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found".Wiz wrote in a blog post, external about its findings that, under the right conditions, hackers could exploit the php2shell issue to take control of affected web servers and steal sensitive data - saying everything built on PHP was left exposed.AI could also make such attacks easier and faster, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC. He estimated the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites.Jill Slay, a cyber-security researcher at the University of Adelaide, said it would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites.What websites have been affected?The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums.That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure.Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website.Image source, EPAImage caption, Websites like the University of Geneva's were taken offline on WednesdayA number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline.Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk.More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said.What happened after the flaws were exposed?The PHP Foundation rolled out patches on Wednesday to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years."All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said.Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms.The US National Security Agency told all organisations that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database."These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said.The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker".Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts.Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP"We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight," Takaichi wrote on X. "If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk," she said.Tech companies have also sought to quickly secure their systems.E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue, but its websites were operating as normal.Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, also said it had seen "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced."That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he wrote on X, external.How was AI involved?Researchers at Calif and Wiz who located the vulnerabilities used advanced AI tools which can analyse code and find flaws much faster than humans or older systems. "Modern software is incredibly complex, and some vulnerabilities can remain undetected for years," Kanhere said."The underlying bugs weren't new; what changed was our ability to find them," Kanhere said.Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform's developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale.The incident "highlights how AI can uncover security flaws" but also how it can "help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post.The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure."Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind," said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre.What does it mean for you?The issue affects back-end website and web development processes that will be invisible to many users - meaning most people won't need to take any action.But small businesses with sites, including those built using WordPress, may be wondering how to protect themselves.Those who own websites or manage infrastructure running PHP have been urged to secure their websites by updating to the latest version.Ethical hacker Ken Munro, who has spent years finding security flaws in computer systems, says installing the fixes - known as patching - is "a bit like running a Windows update".If a hosting company or web developer manages your website, contact them and ask whether the PHP security fixes have been applied - something that must be applied to PHP itself and cannot be resolved by updating WordPress or its plugins.If you look after your website yourself, Munro says "it is your own responsibility to make sure fixes are applied".The UK's National Cyber Security Centre recommends, external considering temporarily taking sites offline if updates or temporary protections cannot be applied quickly enough.The US National Security Agency has also urged "heightened awareness" in the coming weeks, telling people to closely monitor updates from software vendors."Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said, external.And while the onus lies mainly on website operators, users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.He warned people to be alert to any phishing messages exploiting the publicity around the incident too.

schema.headline: PHP: What is it and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble?

title: Surveillance and ‘constant paranoia’: Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow
description: "Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 and 2025, t
body: "Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 and 2025, tells the BBC.US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War.But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year.The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion. They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts, and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials.Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed.Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia."There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty."The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls.Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater."Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow.Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission.The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution".Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials.One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy.Russian officials make little secret of their attitude towards Western diplomats. They have openly accused those from "unfriendly countries" of engaging in "espionage".Moscow has been particularly critical of those who show an interest in expressions of dissent against the Kremlin and, according to Russian journalist Alexei Venediktov, has effectively banned most Russian officials from speaking to Western embassies.This has only worsened relations with the West, says Venediktov, who recalls telling Russian officials: "You are being misunderstood precisely because of your own actions - because ambassadors cannot do their jobs."Today, Moscow has little to no contact with many Western governments, says one ex-European ambassador. "There are no calls, no meetings at ministerial level."But they say this has made diplomats all the more important, left with the responsibility to communicate their governments' positions to Moscow."Generals prove what they can do during a war. The same is true for diplomats. When things get really difficult, every single thing you do actually matters."Lynne Tracy left Moscow in 2025 feeling she had accomplished her primary mission: the US Embassy had held firm.But she is also proud of the work she and her team did to maintain connection between Americans and ordinary Russians."Because at some point, government-to-government relations will have a chance to improve - and those ties between people will be there to help speed the improvement."

schema.headline: Surveillance and ‘constant paranoia’: Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow

title: Married at First Sight Australia: Police investigate show after 'inappropriate' allegations
description: A spokesperson for New South Wales Police Force told BBC News: "On Monday 24 August 2026, officers attached to South Sydney Police Area Command commen
body: A spokesperson for New South Wales Police Force told BBC News: "On Monday 24 August 2026, officers attached to South Sydney Police Area Command commenced an investigation following a report of inappropriate content being shared."Following inquiries, the matter will be referred to WA [Western Australia] Police Force."BBC News has approached WA Police Force, who said the referral has not yet been received.A spokesperson for Channel Nine said: "We are aware of a police investigation involving Endemol Shine Australia and all enquiries should be directed to them."Endemol Shine Australia, which makes MAFS Australia, has not responded to multiple requests for comment over the latest developments.In June, a BBC News investigation heard from nine former cast members from MAFS Australia, who urged the show to improve its background checks and to stop allowing individuals with previous convictions or allegations on the show.One woman from last year's Australian series told us she was not told the man she had been matched with had a previous drug conviction and only found out after the show ended. "There should be informed consent," she told us.Responding to those claims at the time, Channel 9 and Endemol Shine Australia said they had "strong protocols in place to ensure participant safety and wellbeing".As well as being a huge hit in Australia, the show is popular in the UK and is shown on Channel 4.The broadcaster pulled all the UK episodes of MAFS from its streaming service just hours ahead of the transmission of the Panorama investigation in May, but MAFS Australia remains available to watch.In July, BBC News revealed that a cast member from MAFS UK had been arrested on suspicion of rape following the Panorama programme.The individual is not being named; nor is the alleged victim. Anyone who makes an allegation of rape is entitled to anonymity by law.The media regulator Ofcom has also launched an official investigation into the hit  Channel 4 show.The UK version, which has been running for 10 seasons, is one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.The broadcaster has commissioned a review into contributor welfare on the show. However, it only intends to publish "a summary of findings", rather than the full report.Channel 4's chief executive previously said the review was due back in the summer, but it has not yet been published.Speaking to MPs earlier this week, Ofcom boss Dame Melanie Dawes said the report was due back "any day now".BBC News has approached Channel 4 for a response.Lawyers for CPL, the independent production company that makes the UK version of the show, have previously said its welfare system is "gold standard" and industry-leading.If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

title: South Korea: Celebrity shark guided out of Busan canal refuses to swim out to sea
description: A famed dusky shark in South Korea is still lingering near a canal that it was guided out of on Wednesday.The shark, nicknamed Bukangi, became an unli
body: A famed dusky shark in South Korea is still lingering near a canal that it was guided out of on Wednesday.The shark, nicknamed Bukangi, became an unlikely sensation after it was spotted swimming in a canal in the south-eastern port city of Busan last month. For weeks, rescuers tried in vain to get it back to the open sea using large nets. On Thursday, authorities said they had reinforced barriers to prevent Bukangi from returning. But it has yet to swim out into the open sea, and has been circling back repeatedly to the mouth of the waterway.Its rescue prompted mixed reactions in Busan, where some said the shark should stay while others felt it was better for it to go.In a livestreamed operation on Wednesday, rescue workers took more than eight hours to delicately guide the three-metre-long (10ft) shark with a net towards open water in a harbour.Hundreds of adoring fans gathered at the park overlooking the canal, cheering and waving goodbye to the shark.But then, on Thursday morning, Bukangi reportedly swam back into the canal after breaking through a barrier installed by authorities.For some time, Bukangi was trapped in a tight space between two layers of nets in the canal. Rescuers freed it by removing the outer layer, and have since fortified the remaining layer of nets to prevent it from going back in.Since then, authorities said, Bukangi has been swimming further out but keeps circling back.A government official told the BBC on Thursday afternoon that rescuers had concluded their operations to free the shark.It is thought that Bukangi might have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm waters and plenty of fish. With the sea getting warmer each year, experts say Busan may play host to more sharks in the future.In the month that she has been in the canal, Bukangi had already attracted more than 1.6 million visitors.Its popularity gave a welcome boost to Busan's tourism, and the city embraced it as an unofficial mascot.But authorities were also concerned about Bukangi's well-being as it appeared to be injured and was not eating. Social media users have been circulating videos of Bukangi swimming in the canal with what appears to be a bloodied snout.There were concerns the shark would be further weakened by falling water temperatures.Before this week's operation, there had been two earlier failed attempts to guide Bukangi out of the canal with nets.Some in Busan felt it was safer for the shark to remain in the canal. The BBC saw two people holding up cardboard signs protesting against Bukangi's eviction.One of them was Cho Hannah, who had travelled for two hours from her home in North Gyeongsang province to see the shark.Bukangi, she insisted, was "a rare gift" to Busan."This shark has made this canal her home, and we are kicking her out unnecessarily. I am afraid the shark might die tangled with the net, or die out at sea," she said.But others like Yoon In-taek said it was only right that Bukangi left."Bukangi seemed much larger when I first saw her on 18 September, when she first got here. Now she seems gaunt. I'm worried for her health if she stays," he said."It doesn't sit right with me that she keeps returning here. It will be best if Bukangi leaves, doesn't come back, and lives and feeds freely in the open sea. I'd love to see her find a healthy, free life out there," said Shin Seungmin.Bukangi has "brought so much joy to us", he said, adding that he was sad to see her leave."But she should go and live her normal shark life."Additional reporting by Leehyun Choi.

schema.headline: South Korea: Celebrity shark guided out of Busan canal refuses to swim out to sea

title: 'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad
description: Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of the US state of Ohio, has called an attack ad against her that features her estranged mother "desp
body: Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of the US state of Ohio, has called an attack ad against her that features her estranged mother "despicable". Acton commented on the campaign ad from her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, on Wednesday, saying: "This is despicable, what he's done". In the ad Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, says Acton "lied her entire life". But it does not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child and that Acton and her brother were then removed from Arthur's custody.The ad set off a storm of criticism from members of both parties. On Thursday, President Donald Trump sought to defend it and Ramaswamy on social media.Acton and Ramaswamy are both running to replace outgoing Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican who endorsed Ramaswamy, in the 3 November midterm election.In a sign that Ramaswamy may have hurt his chances at winning, DeWine has reportedly described the ad as deeply troubling and called for it to be taken down.  "I've never attacked his family. I would never do that," Acton said about Ramaswamy at the campaign stop on Wednesday evening. "You can see that there are so many people who have experienced trauma and abuse in their lives," she continued, referring to the fallout from the ad. The last time Acton saw her mother was in a courtroom in 1978 after her stepfather was indicted, according to Acton's campaign.Arthur's husband fled the state before he could stand trial, was never prosecuted, and died in 2004. Arthur left with him.In an ad that Acton released earlier this week, her brother recalled their abuse as children and chided Ramaswamy for using sexual assault as "a political talking point".Trump, who has endorsed Ramaswamy,  blamed the press for the negative reaction to the ad, in a long post where he also commended Arthur and Ramaswamy. Trump blasted DeWine, as well.He urged Ramaswamy to keep up his attacks and "let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!""I only wish the mothers of my opponents would be so brave as to come forward and explain that their son or daughter is a liar, and much worse," Trump also posted.In the ad, Arthur repeatedly says Acton lies and asserts she "needs help", but does not discuss anything related to cheating or stealing.Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was reviewing complaints about Ramaswamy's ad, which may have initially aired without a legally required disclaimer to tell viewers who paid for it.Ramaswamy claimed responsibility the day after the ad was released on social media and said his campaign would spend $4m (£3m) to air it across the state.The editorial board of local Ohio news outlet The Columbus Dispatch endorsed Acton after the ad dropped, describing it as "revolting and unsettling".On Thursday, former Republican Ohio Congressman Jim Renacci wrote on X: "The floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor."And any Republican who fails to distance themselves from this ad risks taking on water as well."MK Pritzker, the wife of Illinois' Democratic governor, JB Pritzker, announced on Wednesday that she would donate $500,000 to help Acton in the election.Vice-President JD Vance has said he would like fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about the ad and that he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party.David Lublin, a professor from American University's School of Public Affairs, told the BBC that attack ads are not new in US politics but said "they have become more intense".He suggested Ramaswamy's ad could be an indication that his campaign is desperate to swing momentum in his favour.A poll by VoteHub, external released on Thursday suggested Acton was leading Ramaswamy by 1%, within the margin of error, and noted the surveys were done before the ad.If Acton wins, she would be the first Democrat elected as Ohio governor in two decades.

schema.headline: 'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad

title: V Harish: YouTuber arrested after Indian finance influencer's suicide
description: A 27-year-old finance influencer's suicide in India has been mired in allegations of cyberbullying and started a conversation around who should give f
body: A 27-year-old finance influencer's suicide in India has been mired in allegations of cyberbullying and started a conversation around who should give financial advice to investors.V Harish - who ran a hugely popular Instagram account called "Finance with Harish" - was found dead on Tuesday morning at his home near Chennai, capital of the southern state of Tamil Nadu.His suicide came just weeks after his account was disabled by Meta after complaints of irregularities.In a complaint lodged with the police, his father J Vinayagam has alleged that his son took his life because of online harassment by Jason Samuel, a YouTuber and CEO of tech-centric venture studio Zemuria. Police arrested Samuel on Thursday under suspicion of trying to "extort money from Harish" and posting "defamatory videos against him on social media".BBC Tamil has not been able to reach him for comment. Earlier, he denied wrongdoing in a post on X.The case has brought into focus the growing influence of financial content creators in India, where millions of first-time investors increasingly turn to social media for market advice.Harish began posting videos about finance and investing around five years ago, building a substantial online following.Over the years, he published more than 1,500 videos and amassed more than 1.3 million Instagram followers. He described himself as a financial adviser to "millionaires" and "high-net-worth individuals".He often used music, film clips and photos of global political leaders to make dramatic videos while talking about the rise and fall of the share market and prices of gold and silver.The videos, which broke down financial issues in simple terms, became hugely popular as they coincided with a rapid expansion in India's retail investor base, especially since the 2020 Covid-19 pandemic.The country's largest stock exchange, the National Stock Exchange, said earlier this year it now had more than 130 million unique investors registered with it as opposed to under 30 million in 2019.But in September, Meta took down Harish's Instagram page after receiving complaints he was not registered with Indian market regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) - which is required under law to be able to offer investment advice or manage client portfolios.A back-up account, which gained over 60,000 followers in a short time, was also subsequently taken down, external following complaints from social media users and others.A few other accounts in his name remain on Instagram, though with much smaller followings - and it's not clear who runs them. According to Harish's friends and family, he recorded a video message before his death in which he said that "five years of hard work has been stolen" from him, news channel NDTV reported, external.The video, which has also been shared widely on social media, shows him speaking in Tamil and then switching to English to say "I'm very sorry" to his parents, sister, friends and followers.Police say Harish's father J Vinayagam has blamed "cyberbullying, defamatory social media posts and repeated blocking of his channels" for his son's suicide and named Jason Samuel in his complaint registered at Kanathur police station near Chennai.Samuel had posted a video on his YouTube channel on 18 October questioning Harish's credentials since he did not have Sebi or Amfi (Association of Mutual Funds in India) registrations. In it, he mentioned that Harish's Instagram account had been disabled following complaints.This, Vinayagam says, triggered severe online harassment and led to pressures that drove his son to take his own life. "We demand that a proper investigation be conducted and legal action be taken against Jason Samuel and his accomplices, who spread defamation on social media and caused mental distress through cyberbullying," his complaint states.A police statement says Vinayagam's complaint was registered under "abetment to suicide" and preliminary investigations found Samuel had a "role in this case"."[Samuel] will be produced before court and sent to judicial custody," it says.Samuel has defended the video in which he flagged Harish's lack of credentials saying he was acting in the consumer interest.In a statement on X, Samuel said he was "deeply saddened, heavily grieving, shocked and frozen at what has happened and I mourn the loss of life".He however, rejected allegations of "cyber-bullying" Harish."I have not cyber-bullied him. I pointed out his lack of licence and authority, misrepresentation of licence and fraud... his illegal activity."I literally asked him in the video to come back and do this with a proper Sebi licence. I never intended or expected this drastic measure to happen and I mourn the loss," he wrote.If you're having thoughts of suicide, or know someone that might be, you can find support lines in India via the AASRA website, external or globally via Befrienders Worldwide, external. In the UK you can call the Samaritans Helpline on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org, external.

schema.headline: V Harish: YouTuber arrested after Indian finance influencer's suicide
